# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

## The caches

All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:

- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).

Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

    cd ProjectFortress
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s

Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.

- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.

## Name resolution

- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.

## Building

Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.

- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.

## After an edit of the library

The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.

- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.

## Symptoms of a skipped step

If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:

- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.

If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.

Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:

- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.

Two more facts help you read a run:

- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops

**prompt cache**
: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.

**interrupt**
: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.

**stop of the process**
: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.

**automatic permission check**
: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.

## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.

    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.

- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.

## Stopping processes

Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.

Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.

## After an interrupt or a stop of the process

If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:

1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.

## When the automatic permission check refuses a call

- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).

123	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
124	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
125	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
126	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
127	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
128	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
129	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
130	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

180	## The checker's time
181	
182	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
183	
184	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
185	
186	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
187	
188	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
189	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
190	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
191	
192	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
193	
194	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
195	
196	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
197	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
198	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
199	
200	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
201	
202	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
203	
204	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
205	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
206	
207	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
208	
209	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
210	
211	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
212	
213	If you change the checker:
214	
215	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
216	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
217	
218	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
219	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
220	
221	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
222	4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
223	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
224	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
225	
226	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
227	
228	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
229	
230	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.
231	# The report and the record
232	
233	## What every report holds
234	
235	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
236	
237	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
238	
239	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
240	
241	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
242	
243	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
244	
245	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
246	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
247	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
248	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
249	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
250	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
251	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
252	
253	## At a point to report
254	
255	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
256	- Then finish the work.
257	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
258	
259	## Timings and citations
260	
261	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
262	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
263	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
264	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

266	## POSITIONS and FACTS
267	
268	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
269	
270	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

272	## The gap ledger
273	
274	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
275	
276	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
277	
278	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
279	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
280	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
281	
282	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
283	
284	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
285	
286	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

310	
311	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. 314	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
315	  - what it means for the work;
316	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;

342	
343	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
344	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.

If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.

351	
352	**scratch**
353	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
354	
355	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
356	
357	## What to commit
358	
359	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
360	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
361	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
362	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
363	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
364	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
365	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
366	
367	## How to commit
368	
369	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
370	
371	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
372	
373	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
374	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
375	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
376	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
377	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
378	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
379	
380	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
381	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
382	
383	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
384	
385	## Pushing
386	
387	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
388	
389	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
390	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
391	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
392	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
393	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
394	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
395	
396	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
397	
398	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
399	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
400	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

Sections 1 and 2 were written from the tree, FACTS and the gap ledger before the reviewer read the plan or its grounds. Section 7 and the last section were written after the rehearsal's end, the same day. -->

# The remaining plan against the goal: a review

Paths are under `explorations/` unless they start with `Library/`, `ProjectFortress/`, `Specification/` or `.claude/`. C4 is the flat model program, `run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`, with its vocabulary `FlatArrays` and its loaders `FlatData` beside it. The APL program is `apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`. "The one library" is the interpreter's library, which both paths are to share. "The prelude" is the compiler's own library of three files, which the switch-over deletes.

## 0. What was read and run, and in what order

1. First, with the plan unread: FACTS whole; the model program and its vocabulary; the ledger rows that the model's lines meet (305, 307, 310, 624, 641, 874 and the rows they cite); the kernels report (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`, sections 2 and 4); the code generator's distance report (`perf-probes/codegen-distance/REPORT.md`, section 0); the goal (P-7) with its history. Sections 1 and 2 below were written at that point.
2. One probe of the reviewer's own, before the plan was read, in a worktree seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) and removed after: the compiled checker, by the distance stage's own driver, over microGPT's own import closure against today's one library. Its note is `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/model-closure-check.md`.
3. Then the plan and its grounds: section 3 says what was read.
4. After that, three small programs that pin what the first probe met, a timing of the checker on one program, and a Java model of the library's matrix product (`compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/mul-shape-model.md`).
5. The rehearsal of the switch-over that ran beside this review writes `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`. Section 5 says what of it this review could use.

Machine for the probes: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon 2.30 GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, loads from 0.5 to 2.8, with another worker's runs beside them. A timing here is a measurement only as a ratio of two times taken in one run.

## 1. Where the tree stands

### 1.1 What runs

- **Walk runs microGPT.** Both programs and their quick checks pass the gate's walk check, 7 of 7, in 33 to 39 s (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-30/gate/summary.txt:148-151`).
- **The compiled path runs no array program.** Its prelude has no array type (row 305). `fortress compile` of C4's vocabulary stops at name resolution. No kernel of microGPT's shape has ever run compiled (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`, section 2).
- **The compiled checker accepts the one library.** Over the fourteen components that the default imports reach, it finds 0 errors and no crash (F-53, F-288). That is the first half of the plan, done.
- **The natives are bound for both paths.** 374 of the one library's 402 native bindings name a Java helper that both paths can call. The other 28 are `Reflect`'s, which microGPT does not import (F-299, F-32).

### 1.2 What stands between the checker's zero and a compiled program on the one library

Each line is a thing that the record holds as open, with how well it is known.

- **The code generator has never emitted the one library as it stands.** In the one library's world it refuses `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` whole, at the wrappers of the helper classes that their native bindings name (row 874). The reviewer's probe met the same stop on today's tree: "Can't generate header for method loopChunk with jvm desc =I stripped = FortressLibrary$ZZ32". The count of 38 refused declarations in 10 kinds (F-34) was taken once, on older code, with 288 helper strings put back on walk's glue classes to get past that stop. It is not measured on today's code.
- **No emitted class of the one library has ever been loaded or run** (F-34: "no emitted class was run"). So nothing is known about the class loader on the library's deep generic hierarchy, the run time's built-in value classes (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`, the strings, tuples and arrows) under the one library's names, or the time that a compile and a run take against a library four times the prelude's size (9.4K lines in thirteen components against 2.3K in three).
- **The compiled tests are written against the prelude.** 1,558 compiler tests, 263 other compiler tests and 86 library tests pass against it (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-30/gate/summary.txt:2-3`, `:59`). How many fail against the one library is not measured.
- **microGPT's own files do not check.** Section 5.1 gives today's count: 42 distinct sites in C4's three files, 54 in the APL program's four and one crash in its syntax api, and 25 in two library components that only microGPT's loaders import (`FileSupport`, `File`). Each is a floor, because the checker stops a block at its first failing statement (row 474).
- **Three things that C4's lines need have no compiled form at all.** A size known only at run time, which C4's `view`, `heads` and `unheads` take from `reflect`: a compiled call fails the JVM's verification (row 307). Varargs, which C4's `flat` declares: "Can't compile VarArgs yet" (row 624). An array design: three questions are open with no default (F-270 cites P-85).

### 1.3 What is known about speed

- Under walk, C4's three kernels run 2,500 to 14,000 times slower than Java over `double[]` (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`, section 2). Walk's time goes to walking the tree, not to how numbers are stored.
- A Java model that boxes each number as the compiled run time does, behind a generic array object, runs 2.7 to 6.8 times slower than Java over `double[]` (the same section; F-11). That is the best that today's representation can reach, before anything else that compiled Fortress pays.
- What else it pays is measured only on scalar loops against the prelude: about 31 ns per element, in a transaction check on every read and write of a mutable local, boxing, and a method call per element (F-40, row 641); a generator and a closure call per iteration (F-12).

## 7. After the rehearsal's end (2026-11-10, 15:0x UTC)

The curator took option 3 of finding A: probes first, then the choice between options 1 and 2 (`coordinator/HELD.md`, the lines of 14:0x). The rehearsal's whole report is `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md` at `d381e21775`. The pure-Java microGPT is timed in `java-baseline/python-comparison.md` at `1603d08b49`; its own report was not yet written. This section reads both. Below, A1 is finding A's option 1, the whole switch-over first, and A2 its option 2, the model's slice first.

### 7.1 What the rehearsal settled

- **A program runs compiled against the one library.** With 12 marked hacks, a program that prints a line, one that builds and reads an `Array1`, and a dot product in the program's own loop compile and run, with walk's output. So the first of the two unknowns of section 4.3 has its answer: yes, behind 14 walls.
- **No matrix runs, and none of the library's own array algebra.** Every array of rank 2 dies at `m[i,j]`: the method over the tuple index type has no body at the instantiated descriptor (its W15). The library's `DOT` and `SUM` die on a generic method that an object inherits from another component's trait (its W16). No hack passed either; each needs the code generator's real work. microGPT stops earlier, in the checker, with 17 sites of its own once `I extends Index` is written. That agrees with section 5.1 for `FlatArrays` (7 once the two bounds are written) and for `MicroGptFlat` (8). `FlatData` reads 1 there against 3 here: the compile command stops it at an error of `File`'s api, where the tolerant driver checks on.
- **Of the 16 walls, nine things are in no line of PLAN** (its section 6, last paragraph): the carrier design beyond N5's table, the team's search by the prelude's names in the trait table, the package in `OverloadSet`, `NN32`'s two getters, the methods written twice into 27 classes, the verifier's count over the emitted library, rows 624, 81 and 315 on the path of a one-line program, the tuple index type as the wall of every matrix, and the new library order of fourteen compiles.
- **The walls are of two kinds, and the kinds decide the sizes below.**
  - *Walls that a test against the prelude can show today.* They are the code generator's, each with a row whose reproducer runs in the prelude's world: varargs (row 624), `label` and `exit` (row 81), a closure class written twice (row 315), a method written twice with the wrong forwarder (row 571's kind), the missing cast at a `comprises` type (rows 307 and 695), the tuple index's bridge (row 832's kind), the inherited generic method (rows 495, 496, 732), and the rest of the 24 refused declarations (rows 822, 812, 819, 540, 875). In rungs, 11 to 15: the rehearsal's own count for the first seven kinds, and one each for the other four refused kinds.
  - *Walls that only the switch shows.* The carriers, which are a design first and then about three rungs, and which reach into the code generator's naming (its W2, W12, W13, W14); the trait table's search (W3); `OverloadSet`'s four names (W11); the code generator's stop on `NN32`'s getters (W4); seven more source files that name the prelude; the library order. About seven rungs and one decision of the curator's, which the rehearsal puts as its question: which run-time class carries each built-in type.
- **One build serves one library.** The run time's thirteen value classes extend the prelude's generated classes by name in their Java source. So the walls of the second kind cannot be gated on `main` before the switch, unless those classes exist twice.

### 7.2 The sizes of A1 and A2 now

The unit is a batch with its landing, 5M to 14M tokens by the record. Phase 4 has landed at most three rungs that edit `CodeGen.java` in one batch (climb batch 30's record put a rung into its second run because the first "already has three rungs in `CodeGen.java`": `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-30.md`, "Why two runs"), so the 11 to 15 rungs of the first kind are 3 to 5 batches under either option. The milestone is the same for both: a matrix and the library's own `DOT` run compiled against the one library, in a landed tree, under the gate. Each number is an estimate from the rehearsal's rungs, not a plan.

**A1, the whole switch-over first.**

1. The code generator's rungs that the prelude can test: 3 to 5 batches.
2. Then one landing that holds everything that only the switch shows, because, by the rehearsal's W2, the prelude's programs stop running once the value classes are re-parented: the carriers with the rungs around them, about seven in all, the verifier's count and what it finds, all 1,907 compiled tests moved or respelled, and the prelude's deletion. The record's bound for it was "at least two gated batches". The rehearsal met 16 walls on the way to three small programs, so 3 to 5 is the fairer range. It lands whole or not at all, and nothing in it is gated before it lands. The batch workflow has no form for it: a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, and these walls stand one behind the other.
3. The milestone: after 6 to 10 batches, 30M to 140M tokens. microGPT's own needs follow (the model's sized types, run-time sizes, `File` and `FileSupport`, the tuple binding, the numeral tie): 1 or 2 batches more.

**A2, the model's slice first.**

1. The same 3 to 5 batches of code-generator rungs.
2. Beside them, in the same batches, since they touch other files: the carriers built as a second set of the thirteen value classes, chosen by the world that the compile command and the run select; the tables, the two converters and the 99 raise strings made to follow that choice; the rungs around them; a second library order and one test track against the one library in the gate. That is the seven rungs of A1's step 2 and 2 or 3 more for the second set: 2M to 4M tokens more than A1 in all. From then on, `Hello` and the `Array1` program are gated tests, and every later wall is one rung with its own test on the one library.
3. The milestone: after 3 to 5 batches, 15M to 70M tokens. microGPT's own needs: 1 or 2 batches more.
4. The tests' move and the prelude's deletion: the same work as in A1, 2 to 5 batches by the same reasoning, but beside or after the model, test by test, with the gate green throughout.

**What separates them.** Not the total: A2 is A1 plus two or three rungs, about 200 s more in every gate for the second library order, and a prelude that lives until the end. What separates them is where the unknown work sits. In A1 the walls that only the switch shows, and whatever the 1,907 tests uncover, sit inside one landing that cannot be gated in parts. In A2 they are met one at a time on `main`. The rehearsal showed how such walls behave: eight of its sixteen were seen only under the switch (its W1 to W4 and W11 to W14), each stood behind the one before it, and one hack (keeping the first copy of a method written twice) ran once and then failed after an unrelated rebuild.

### 7.3 What the first compiled timing says, and what it cannot say

The timing (the rehearsal's section 5): the loop `s += a[i] b[i]` over two arrays of 1,000 `RR64`, run 5,000 times, 5 million iterations. Compiled against the one library, 1.4 s with the JVM's start; a one-line program takes 0.6 s, so about 0.8 s for the loop. Under walk, 39.8 s, about 36 s for the loop.

For the Java side, this review ran the same loop in plain Java on this machine (not in the rehearsal's run, at a load of 1.7 to 2.4): 7.2 ms for the first pass in a cold JVM, 2.5 to 6.1 ms for the next four.

**What it says.**

- Compiled code on the one library is about 45 times faster than walk on this loop.
- It is of the order of a hundred times slower than Java: 0.8 s against 7 ms cold, which is about 110 times, and more against a warm pass. Per iteration, about 160 ns against about 1 ns.
- Boxing does not explain that distance. The Java models of the compiled run time's boxes behind a generic array put boxing at about 7 times on a dot product (F-11). So a factor of 15 or more stands in what the one library and the generated code put between the loop and the array: the read through the store's native wrapper, with a check of the thread and the transaction on every access and a `cast` on every read (F-333; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 6), the sequential range's closure for each iteration, and the transaction check and the box on the accumulator (row 641). None of these has a measured share. The nearest numbers on file, from other sessions and on the prelude, are 37 ns an iteration for a scalar loop (F-12) and 31 ns an element for a loop over the prelude's vector (F-40).
- For scale: one training step of the pure-Java microGPT is 0.113 ms, about 200K multiply-adds (`java-baseline/python-comparison.md`, section 1). At 160 ns for each, the same arithmetic written as plain loops over rank-1 arrays would take about 32 ms a step, some 280 times the baseline. That is arithmetic on one timing, not a forecast: the model is not written as plain loops, and section 5.2's factor for the library's matrix product comes on top.

**What it cannot say.**

- Nothing about steady state. The compiled loop ran for 0.8 s in all, with the JIT's warm-up inside it.
- Nothing certain as a ratio. It is one run, not a pair, on a machine at a load of 3.7 to 4.8 on four CPUs.
- Nothing about unboxed numbers. Every number in it is a box; decisions A and B are not built. The verifier was off, which bears on loading, not on the loop.
- Nothing about microGPT's kernels. It is rank 1, in the program's own loop. No matrix, no view, no `mul`, no library reduction and no parallel loop ran.

So the second unknown of section 4.3 has a first, rough answer: today's distance to Java is about two orders of magnitude before the library's own algorithms are counted, and most of it is not boxing. That makes phase 6 a larger piece than its list in PLAN shows, and it is one more reason to have a compiled kernel under the gate early, where each of these costs can be measured and removed.

### 7.4 Which further probe would decide between A1 and A2

- **Probe Y, the second set, in scratch.** On the rehearsal's patch, keep the prelude's value classes, add the re-parented set beside them, make the tables follow the world, and show one build that runs `Hello` against the prelude and against the one library. One worker's session, about 1M to 1.5M tokens. It decides whether A2 exists at the cost given above. If it fails, A1 is the only road.
- **Probe X, the compiled tests against the scratch switch.** Run the three compiled test tracks on the rehearsal's tree, with fixed-arity stand-ins for the varargs `assert`, and sort what fails. One or two sessions, 1.5M to 3M tokens. It gives A1's single landing its size. It is worth its cost only if probe Y fails, or if the curator leans to A1 after it.
- **Not a probe for this choice, but for phase 6:** a profile of the rehearsal's dot loop, to split the 160 ns among the store's check, the cast, the range and the accumulator. One session, under 1M. It would turn 7.3's list into shares.

Probe Y is worth its cost: about 1M against a choice that governs at least three batches of difference and where the unknown work lands.

### 7.5 Whether the recommendations change

- **A.** Changed. Before the rehearsal's end the recommendation after the probes was option 1 with the names work done first as a step of its own. The rehearsal shows that the names work cannot land first on its own: one build serves one library. Done first, it is option 2's second set. So the recommendation now is **A2, if probe Y shows the second set running both libraries from one build; A1 if it does not, with probe X run before its single landing is planned.** A2 costs two or three rungs more and keeps the prelude longer, which P-37 calls a bootstrap to remove; it does not add a declaration to the prelude, and the deletion stays the plan's end. The curator's first decision on either road is the rehearsal's question on the carriers.
- **B.** Sharper, and its options 2 and 3 are now one. Climb batch 30b waits for Friday's reset by his word of 14:0x. The next batch should be cut from the rehearsal's first kind of wall, the code generator's rungs that a test against the prelude can show: varargs, `label`, the closure class, the methods written twice, the cast at a `comprises` type, the tuple index's bridge, the inherited generic method. Of climb batch 30b's own content it keeps the `atomic` expression, which is one of the 24 refusals (row 875), the field inside a transaction, and the numeral rule in the checker, whose tests are now two model lines: `MicroGptFlat.fss:82` and `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss:40`. The top-level tuple binding of section 5.1 joins it. `tryatomic`, row 322's remainder and the numerals' parser leftovers move behind the milestone.
- **C.** Unchanged: option 2, the matrix product's grain on phase 6's list, built with the first compiled kernel. Two things strengthen it. The first compiled timing puts element access itself at about 160 ns, so `mul`'s shape is not the first cost to remove. And the Java baseline's worker is building a variant in the library's fork/join shape (the coordinator's message of 2026-11-10), which will measure in the baseline program what `mul-shape-model.md` only models; that note is then superseded.

Two lines of section 6.2 change with the rehearsal's end. Line 1 holds, with its sizes: the names work is a design and about seven rungs, not one. Line 4 gains the rehearsal's count for C4 under the compile command itself: 17 sites with the index bound written.
